David Clarkson
DAY-vid KLARK-suhn
proper noun
Hebrew given name David, “beloved”; the surname Clarkson, “son of the clerk” or scholar.

📖 Biblical Definition

David Clarkson (1622–1686) was a Puritan minister and scholar, educated at Cambridge, who labored faithfully through the upheavals of his age and was ejected in 1662 with the host of Nonconformist ministers who would not bow to the Act of Uniformity. In his later years he served as colleague and then successor to the great John Owen at the congregation in London, no small honor, for Owen esteemed him highly. Clarkson was a preacher of uncommon weight and a theologian of careful judgment, and several of his sermons endure as choice Puritan divinity. Best known among them is Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven, a piercing exposure of the idolatry that lurks not in carved images alone but in the heart’s inward esteeming, trusting, loving, and fearing of any thing above God. Clarkson showed that whatever the soul prizes more than the LORD, whatever it makes its chief good or its refuge, becomes an idol that bars the gate of heaven. His doctrine pressed the first commandment inward upon the conscience, leaving no covert for secret idols. A man of learning and piety, Clarkson stands among those faithful pastors whom the church remembers chiefly through their printed sermons, ministering still to readers the searching, God-exalting truth they once preached to congregations now long gathered home.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An ejected Puritan minister and successor to John Owen, remembered for the sermon Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven.

expand to see more

DAVID CLARKSON, English Puritan minister and scholar (1622–1686), educated at Clare College, Cambridge.

Ejected in 1662 for refusing conformity to the Act of Uniformity.

Colleague and successor of John Owen at his London congregation.

Author of the sermon Soul-Idolatry Excludes Men Out of Heaven.

He exposed inward idolatry of heart as the secret transgression of the first commandment (Eze 14:3).

📖 Key Scripture

Eze 14:3 — "Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be inquired of at all by them?"

Col 3:5 — "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:"

1Jo 5:21 — "Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen."

Exo 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Clarkson’s doctrine of soul-idolatry is recovered against an age that confines idolatry to ancient statues and never suspects the idols of the heart.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Clarkson’s great theme rebukes the modern conceit that idolatry is a primitive sin of carved images, long since outgrown. Clarkson showed that the heart is a perpetual factory of idols, and that to love, trust, fear, or esteem any thing—wealth, reputation, pleasure, self—above God is soul-idolatry, the inward breaking of the first commandment. The polished modern who scoffs at heathen shrines may yet bow before idols of his own affection.

The lesson to recover is that worship is the deepest act of the soul, and that whatever it makes its chief good it makes its god. Clarkson presses the conscience to ask not merely what it bows before in temples but what it cherishes, relies upon, and dreads to lose. The remedy is to dethrone every rival and to give to God alone the supreme love, trust, and fear that are His due.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

David means “beloved”; Clarkson means “son of the clerk,” the scholar.

expand to see more

David — from Hebrew Dawid, “beloved.”

Clarkson, “son of the clerk,” from clerk, anciently a learned man or cleric.

Idol, from the Greek eidōlon, “an image, a phantom,” a false object of worship.

Idolatry, the service or worship rendered to an idol, whether outward or inward (Col 3:5).

Mortify, from the Latin mortificare, “to put to death,” as the saint must slay his idols.

Usage

"David Clarkson preached that the heart’s secret idols shut men out of heaven."

"John Owen esteemed David Clarkson enough to make him his colleague and successor."

"After his ejection, David Clarkson’s searching sermons endured in print."
